segments.text: AI chatbots are programmed to sound patient, caring, and understanding.
But because there is a strict limit to what a language model can actually do,
we have to consider what happens when kind words aren't enough.
Take the example of a high school student sharing a common vulnerability,
telling a chat interface,
I've been eating lunch alone for like two weeks.
If that student tells their older sister, she might say,
come sit with me in just tomorrow.
That is a person hearing a problem and taking an action.
Tomorrow, she will look for them,
and the reality of that lunch will physically change.
A chatbot will reply with a different focus.
It might say, I'm sorry, eating alone can feel isolating.
Would you like strategies for connecting with classmates?
The AI provides validating words, but it cannot show up to the cafeteria.
Nothing changes outside the chat window.
This is the support trap,
the mistake of confusing supportive language with actual, actionable support.
To navigate these situations, use AI to get ready for people, not replace them.
On the left, the tool can help organize your thoughts or rehearse conversations.
On the right, a machine cannot take responsibility, show up, or check on you tomorrow.
This framework centers on preparation, not substitution.
Sometimes that preparation is the only step required.
If you just need to vent, putting an ordinary frustration into words can help you cool down.
In those cases, the job safely ends in the chat.
In other cases, AI helps you prepare for an action,
like drafting an email to a teacher or practicing a talk with your parents.
This is useful only if you take the final step to actually send that message or speak to that person.
This process of refining a message must stop if there is a safety risk.
If someone may be unsafe, you have to leave the chat immediately and find a person who has the capacity to act.
Please note, the following story discusses suicide.
In 2025, Laura Riley wrote about her daughter, Sophie Rotenberg.
Sophie had spent months sharing thoughts she hid from the people around her with a chat GPT persona she called Harry.
The chatbot responded with warmth and occasionally encouraged Sophie to seek help,
but the software was trapped in the interface.
It could not alert her therapist, contact her family, or bring anyone into the room.
After Sophie died, her mother described the chats as a black box.
Pouring distress into an AI creates a false sense of communication,
which can hide the severity of a crisis from the people who have the power to intervene.
There is a specific protocol to follow if someone may be in danger.
First, leave the chat.
Tell a trusted adult or school counselor.
In the US, you can call or text 988 for crisis support or call 911 if the danger is immediate.
Second, do it now.
Do not wait for one more message.
A chatbot cannot protect anyone or carry responsibility for their safety.
Third, tell anyway.
You might hesitate if you promise to keep a secret, but you must involve an adult regardless.
Safety outranks secrecy.
When danger is present, the very next move must reach a person who can act.
Most of AI literacy is about how to use tools well.
Here, using the tool well means knowing when to leave the chat.
AI can help you get ready for people.
In danger, leave the chat and bring in someone who can act.
